title: Graz in a day: the Kunsthaus, the armoury, the Schlossberg, and what the Joanneum 24-hour ticket covers
subtitle: A free hill, an arsenal of 32,000 weapons, a blue bubble of a museum, and one ticket that opens nineteen doors.
excerpt: What is free in Graz and what needs a ticket: the three ways up the Schlossberg, what you see in the Landeszeughaus and the Kunsthaus, and when the 24-hour ticket of the Universalmuseum Joanneum is the one to buy.

is the Schlossberg in Graz free
is the Kunsthaus Graz worth visiting
is the Styrian Armoury open in winter
how long do you need in Graz
meta_title: Graz: Kunsthaus, armoury, Schlossberg, Joanneum ticket
meta_description: What is free in Graz and what needs a ticket: the Schlossberg, the Landeszeughaus, the Kunsthaus, and what the Joanneum 24-hour ticket covers.

featured_image.alt: The blue, bubble-shaped Kunsthaus Graz among the red tiled roofs of the town, seen from the Schlossberg above

content_html:
[place attraction="kunsthaus-graz" city="graz"]

In the summer of 1809 a French force besieged the fortress on the Schlossberg, the wooded rock in the middle of Graz. The garrison, a few hundred men under Major Franz Hackher, held out for weeks and was never taken. It made no difference. Austria lost the war, and the peace signed that autumn obliged it to pull the fortress down. The walls were blown up over the following winter.

Two towers were spared, because the people of Graz paid for them: 2,987 gulden and 11 kreuzer bought the clock tower and the bell tower. The clock tower, the Uhrturm, is now the emblem of the city, and the ruined hill around it is a public park. Most of what you will want to see in Graz lies within fifteen minutes' walk of it, and only a few doors ask for a ticket.

The Schlossberg: free, with three ways up

The hill rises about 120 metres above the main square. On top are the clock tower, the bell tower of 1588 with a bell the city calls Liesl, bastions, cafés, and views over the red roofs in every direction. All of it is open ground.

  • The steps. From Schlossbergplatz 260 steps zigzag up the rock face. They were cut during the First World War.
  • The lift. A glass lift runs up inside the hill from the same square, through tunnels dug as air-raid shelters in the Second World War. It has its own fare.
  • The funicular. The Schlossbergbahn has climbed the north-western side since 1894. The city transport company runs it, and ordinary city tickets have been valid on it.

Look closely at the clock. The long hand shows the hours and the short one the minutes: the tower first had only an hour hand, large enough to read from the town, and the minute hand was added later.

The Uhrturm. The long hand shows the hours. Photo: Taxiarchos228, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

The Landeszeughaus, the armoury

In the seventeenth century Styria was border country, raided from Ottoman territory, and the Styrian estates kept weapons ready for the men they could call up. Between 1642 and 1645 they built an arsenal on Herrengasse to hold them. A century later, when Empress Maria Theresa wanted such depots cleared out, the estates asked to keep theirs as a memorial, and she agreed.

So it is still there: about 32,000 pieces on four floors, on the original wooden racks. Armour for men and horses, helmets by the hundred, pikes, swords, muskets, pistols and cannon. It is usually described as the largest historic armoury in the world to survive as it was. Very little is labelled: you are walking through a store, not an exhibition. Allow an hour.

The building is unheated. In the cold months it has been open only on guided tours and on fewer days, so check the season before you count on it. Next door, the arcaded Renaissance courtyard of the Landhaus, begun in 1557, is free to walk into.

A corridor of the Landeszeughaus, with armour on its original racks. Photo: Tudoi61, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Kunsthaus

Across the river Mur stands the building locals call the Friendly Alien: a blue bubble of acrylic panels by the architects Peter Cook and Colin Fournier, opened in 2003, the year Graz was European Capital of Culture. It grows out of the Eisernes Haus, a cast-iron building of 1848, and after dark lamps under the skin turn the river side into a coarse screen.

What is inside matters for your decision. The Kunsthaus has no collection of its own on permanent show. It stages changing exhibitions of contemporary art, so a visit is as good as the current one: look it up first. The building itself you can enjoy for nothing from the river bank and from the Schlossberg.

A few steps upstream floats the Murinsel, a shell of steel and glass by the New York artist Vito Acconci, also from 2003, with a café and a small open-air theatre. Footbridges join it to both banks, and crossing is free.

The Murinsel of 2003, free to walk across. Photo: Leonhard Lenz, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

What the Joanneum 24-hour ticket covers

The armoury and the Kunsthaus both belong to the Universalmuseum Joanneum, founded by Archduke Johann in 1811 and the oldest public museum in Austria. It sells one ticket for all its houses, valid for 24 hours from the first entry. Our partner's listing counts nineteen. In Graz it names:

  • the armoury and the Kunsthaus;
  • the Joanneum quarter, five minutes south of the main square: the Neue Galerie (art from the nineteenth century to now), the Natural History Museum and a science centre for young people;
  • the History Museum and the Folk Life Museum;
  • at Schloss Eggenberg, on the western edge of the city: the Alte Galerie of old masters, the Archaeology Museum and the Coin Cabinet.

The rest are out in Styria.

Three things to know

  • Twenty-four hours can span two days. Start after lunch and the ticket still works the next morning.
  • The partner's voucher is exchanged for the real ticket at the desk of the Kunsthaus, the armoury, the Natural History Museum or the Neue Galerie.
  • Audio guides and guided tours are listed as not included. The listing does not say plainly whether the state rooms of Schloss Eggenberg, which are shown on guided tours and only in season, count. Ask before you ride out there.

Most of the houses have been closed on Mondays. With one museum in mind, buy its single ticket. With two or more, compare the sum with the 24-hour ticket.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Kunsthaus Graz entry ticket is admission to the exhibitions. The listing speaks of a permanent collection, but see above.
  • The Landeszeughaus entry ticket is admission and a printed visitor's guide from the desk, plus the guided tour in the months when that is the only way in.
  • The self-guided audio walk is a route of about two hours in the partner's app, on your own phone, from Schlossbergplatz over the hill, past the Murinsel and the Kunsthaus, to the cathedral and the main square. It includes no entry anywhere.

These are the tickets and the audio walk our partner sells for Graz, with today's prices:

[partner city="graz" match="kunsthaus,landeszeughaus,joanneum" limit="4"]

A day in order

Start on the Hauptplatz and walk down Herrengasse to the Landhaus courtyard and the armoury. Go up Sporgasse to the cathedral and the mausoleum of Emperor Ferdinand II beside it, then find the double spiral staircase of about 1500 in the Burg across the street, which is free. After lunch cross the Murinsel to the Kunsthaus. Keep the Schlossberg for late afternoon. Current hours are on our pages for the Styrian Armoury, the Kunsthaus Graz and the clock tower.

The Hauptplatz, with the Schlossberg and its clock tower above. Photo: Isiwal, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

From here

Schloss Eggenberg is about twenty minutes away by tram. The palace of 1625 was planned as a calendar in stone, with 365 outside windows and 24 state rooms, and peacocks walk in its park. Direct trains from Vienna take about two and a half hours, over the Semmering line of 1854. See what else there is in Graz, or open the trip planner for Austria.

Cover photo: Marion Schneider & Christoph Aistleitner, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5.

faqs.q: What does the Joanneum 24-hour ticket include?
faqs.a: Entry to the houses of the Universalmuseum Joanneum in Graz and Styria for 24 hours from first use, among them the Landeszeughaus, the Kunsthaus, the Neue Galerie and the museums at Schloss Eggenberg. Audio guides and guided tours are extra.

faqs.q: Is the Schlossberg in Graz free?
faqs.a: Yes. The hill, the outside of the clock tower and the views cost nothing. You pay only if you ride up by lift or funicular; the 260 steps are free.

faqs.q: Is the Kunsthaus Graz worth visiting?
faqs.a: It depends on the current exhibition, because the Kunsthaus has no permanent display of its own. The building can be admired free from the river bank and from the Schlossberg.

faqs.q: Is the Styrian Armoury open in winter?
faqs.a: In the cold months it has been open only on guided tours and on fewer days, because the building is unheated. Check the season before you plan around it.

faqs.q: How long do you need in Graz?
faqs.a: One full day covers the Schlossberg, the armoury, the old town and the Kunsthaus. Add half a day for Schloss Eggenberg.

title: The Hofburg in Vienna on foot: what is free to walk through, and which door needs which ticket
subtitle: A palace with no front door and no single ticket: the free route through its courtyards, and what is behind each paid entrance.
excerpt: The Hofburg is a public thoroughfare with half a dozen separate museums in it. The free walk from Michaelerplatz to Heldenplatz, what the Imperial Treasury, the Sisi Museum and the Kunsthistorisches Museum each show, and what the partner tickets include.
longtail_phrases: can you walk through the Hofburg for free
is there one ticket for the whole Hofburg
Imperial Treasury or Sisi Museum which is better
how long do you need at the Kunsthistorisches Museum
where is the entrance to the Imperial Treasury in Vienna
meta_title: Hofburg Vienna on foot: what is free, which ticket
meta_description: The free walk through the Hofburg courtyards, and what the Imperial Treasury, the Sisi Museum and the Kunsthistorisches Museum each need a ticket for.

featured_image.alt: The curved white St Michael's Wing of the Hofburg in Vienna with its green copper dome, seen across Michaelerplatz

content_html:
[place attraction="hofburg-palace" city="vienna"]

The Hofburg was never finished. It began as a castle in the thirteenth century, and for more than six hundred years each generation of Habsburgs added a wing, a chapel, a library or a riding school to whatever stood there already. The last and largest piece, the Neue Burg, was completed in 1913. It was meant to face a twin across the square, in a forum that would have reached the two great museums beyond the Ring. Five years later the monarchy was gone, and the twin was never built.

What remains is less a palace than a small district: eighteen wings and nineteen courtyards, by the usual count, with streets running through them. The President of Austria has his office here. So do the National Library, a riding school, a conference centre and several museums, each run by a different body with its own desk. There is no front door and no single ticket. The good news is that the best walk through it costs nothing.

What is free: the walk through

The passages and courtyards are public ground, open at all hours. From Michaelerplatz to the Ring takes fifteen minutes without stops.

  • Michaelerplatz. Roman and medieval foundations lie open in the middle of the square. Opposite the palace stands the plain Looshaus of 1911, a scandal in its day.
  • The rotunda under the dome. The gate of St Michael's Wing, finished in 1893, leads into a round hall. The entrance to the imperial apartments is here.
  • In der Burg. The inner courtyard, with a monument to Emperor Francis I. On one side is the Swiss Gate of 1552, painted red and dark grey. Go through it to the oldest court, the Schweizerhof, for the Treasury and the palace chapel.
  • Heldenplatz. The square of the two riders: Archduke Charles, whose horse balances on its hind legs alone, and Prince Eugene. From the balcony of the Neue Burg Hitler announced the annexation of Austria on 15 March 1938.
  • Josefsplatz, on the other flank, in front of the library, and the Burggarten and Volksgarten, the two palace gardens, now public parks.
  • The Augustinian Church, the court's parish church, where Franz Joseph married Elisabeth in 1854. Inside is Canova's marble tomb for Archduchess Marie Christine. Entry is free outside services.

The Swiss Gate of 1552. The way to the Treasury leads through it. Photo: Didi43, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Imperial Treasury

Through the Swiss Gate and up a stair. Twenty-one dim rooms hold the regalia of two empires. The Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire was made in the second half of the tenth century and was used for coronations until 1792. The crown of Rudolf II, of 1602, became the crown of the Austrian Empire two centuries later. Around them are the Holy Lance, the treasure of the Order of the Golden Fleece, the cradle made for Napoleon's son, a narwhal tusk long shown as the horn of a unicorn, and an agate bowl once taken for the Holy Grail.

Allow an hour to an hour and a half. It has been closed on Tuesdays.

The Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire, in the Treasury. Photo: Gryffindor, via Wikimedia Commons.

The Sisi Museum and the imperial apartments

One ticket, one route, entered under the dome: first a museum about Empress Elisabeth, with her dresses, portraits and the story of her murder in Geneva in 1898, then the rooms where she and Franz Joseph lived and worked. His study and iron bed are as plain as the legend says. It is the busiest door in the palace. Our partner does not sell this ticket. Buy it from the palace itself.

The other doors

  • The State Hall of the National Library, on Josefsplatz: a Baroque hall of the 1720s, nearly eighty metres long, with some 200,000 old books under a painted dome. Its own ticket, and worth half an hour.
  • The Spanish Riding School: the white Lipizzaner stallions, in a riding hall of 1735. Performances and morning exercise are sold separately by the school.
  • The palace chapel, where the Vienna Boys' Choir sings Sunday mass for much of the year. Seats are ticketed.
  • The Neue Burg: the Weltmuseum, the imperial armoury, a collection of historic musical instruments and finds from Ephesus.

The partner sells none of these four.

The Neue Burg on Heldenplatz, finished in 1913, with the statue of Prince Eugene. Photo: C.Stadler/Bwag, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 AT.

The Kunsthistorisches Museum

Cross the Ring from Heldenplatz and you stand between two identical domed buildings with Maria Theresa on a monument between them. The one on the left as you face them is the museum of art history, opened in 1891 to hold what the Habsburgs had collected. Its picture gallery has the largest group of Bruegels anywhere, among them The Tower of Babel and Hunters in the Snow, with Vermeer's Art of Painting, Raphael, Titian, Caravaggio and the infantas of Velázquez. Downstairs are the Kunstkammer, with Cellini's golden salt cellar, and the Egyptian rooms. On the main staircase, look up for early paintings by Gustav Klimt between the arches.

Allow two to three hours. It has been closed on Mondays for part of the year. The museum and the Treasury belong to the same institution, which has sold a combined ticket at its own desks.

Pieter Bruegel the Elder, The Tower of Babel, 1563, in the Kunsthistorisches Museum. Photo: Google Art Project, via Wikimedia Commons.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Imperial Treasury ticket with a city sights audio tour is entry to the Treasury and an audio walk of about three kilometres from the Schweizerhof to St Stephen's Cathedral. The listing says there is no commentary inside the Treasury.
  • The Kunsthistorisches Museum ticket with a highlights audio tour is an open-dated entry and a route with commentary inside the museum, in the partner's app. It is the only one of the six with a guide indoors. Bring earphones.
  • The walking audio tour around the Hofburg starts at the plague column on the Graben and ends on Albertinaplatz, an hour for two kilometres. Its listing states that tickets to the palace are not included.
  • The audio walk through imperial Vienna covers much the same courtyards and ends near Karlsplatz. The partner lists several walks under this one title.
  • Two longer audio tours, "Imperial Elegance" and "Art and Imperial Splendor", range across the city as far as the Belvedere, and one of them as far as Schönbrunn. They are not walks around the Hofburg, whatever the name suggests.

These are the tickets and audio walks our partner sells around the Hofburg, with today's prices:

[partner city="vienna" match="hofburg,treasury,kunsthistorisches,imperial" limit="6"]

Which door, if you pay for only one

  • Crowns, relics and a thousand years of empire: the Treasury.
  • The private life of the last emperors: the Sisi Museum and apartments.
  • Paintings: the Kunsthistorisches Museum, with half a day.
  • Nothing at all: the walk above, with the church and the two gardens, fills a good hour.

Hours are on our pages for the Hofburg, the Imperial Treasury and the Kunsthistorisches Museum.

From here

The Albertina stands at the southern tip of the palace, and the State Opera is just beyond it. Behind the museums lies the MuseumsQuartier, in the former imperial stables. See what else there is in Vienna, or open the trip planner for Austria.

Cover photo: Tilman2007, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Can you walk through the Hofburg for free?
faqs.a: Yes. The passages, courtyards and squares of the Hofburg are public ground, open at all hours, and so are the Burggarten and the Volksgarten. You pay only to enter the museums.

faqs.q: Is there one ticket for the whole Hofburg?
faqs.a: No. The Sisi Museum and apartments, the Imperial Treasury, the State Hall of the library, the Spanish Riding School and the museums of the Neue Burg each sell their own ticket.

faqs.q: Imperial Treasury or Sisi Museum: which should you choose?
faqs.a: The Treasury for crowns, relics and the history of the empire, in quiet rooms. The Sisi Museum and apartments for the private life of Franz Joseph and Elisabeth, on a busier route.

faqs.q: How long do you need at the Kunsthistorisches Museum?
faqs.a: Two to three hours for the picture gallery and the Kunstkammer. The Imperial Treasury takes an hour to an hour and a half.

faqs.q: Where is the entrance to the Imperial Treasury in Vienna?
faqs.a: In the Schweizerhof, the oldest courtyard of the Hofburg. Walk through the red and dark grey Swiss Gate from the courtyard called In der Burg.

title: St. Pauli in Hamburg: the Reeperbahn by day and by night, the old Elbe tunnel, and what is free
subtitle: A rope walk that became an entertainment mile, a tunnel under the river that costs nothing, and one museum ship worth boarding.
excerpt: What the Reeperbahn is like by day and by night, how the Old Elbe Tunnel and the Landungsbrücken work, what you see on the Rickmer Rickmers, what is free in St. Pauli, and what the partner tickets and audio walks include.
focus_keyword: Reeperbahn by day or by night
secondary_keywords: what is free in St. Pauli
longtail_phrases: is the Reeperbahn worth visiting during the day
is the Old Elbe Tunnel free
is the Rickmer Rickmers worth it
where did the Beatles play in Hamburg
is the Reeperbahn safe at night
meta_title: St. Pauli Hamburg: Reeperbahn, Elbe tunnel, what is free
meta_description: The Reeperbahn by day and by night, the free Old Elbe Tunnel, the Landungsbrücken and the Rickmer Rickmers: what to pay for in St. Pauli and what not.

featured_image.alt: The green three-masted museum ship Rickmer Rickmers moored at the Hamburg waterfront, with the copper tower of St Michael's Church behind

content_html:
[place attraction="rickmer-rickmers" city="hamburg"]

A sailing ship needs rope by the kilometre, and rope has to be twisted in a straight line. So every port had a rope walk, a long narrow strip of ground where the ropemakers paced backwards with the strands. Hamburg's lay outside the western gate, on the open land between the city and the neighbouring town of Altona, which belonged to the Danish crown. In Low German a rope is a Reep. The strip was the Reeperbahn.

The same ground between two jurisdictions drew everything the city did not want inside its walls: noisy trades, hospitals, and from the late eighteenth century the booths of showmen and the taverns that lived off sailors with pay in their pockets. The suburb took the name of its church, St. Pauli. The ropemakers left, and the name stayed on a street of about 900 metres that is still the best-known in Germany. The river is a short walk away, and most of what is worth doing between the two costs nothing.

The Reeperbahn by day

In daylight the street is plain, a little worn, and easy to read. Walk it from east to west.

  • Spielbudenplatz. The name means the square of the show booths. It is still lined with theatres, among them the St. Pauli Theater, founded in 1841, and the Panoptikum, a waxworks open since 1879.
  • The Davidwache. A brick police station of 1914 by Fritz Schumacher, the city's great architect, on the corner of Davidstraße.
  • Herbertstraße. A short street of brothel windows, closed off by screens at both ends since the 1930s. Signs ask women and anyone under 18 to stay out.
  • Große Freiheit. The "great freedom" in the name was freedom of trade and of religion, which Altona granted when Hamburg did not. That is why a Baroque Catholic church stands in the middle of the clubs.
  • Beatles-Platz. A round black square laid out like a record in 2008, with steel outlines of the band.

Beatles-Platz, where Große Freiheit meets the Reeperbahn. Photo: Bernhard Diener, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Beatles, briefly

The band arrived in August 1960, five of them, and played their first Hamburg nights at the Indra, at the far end of Große Freiheit, before moving down the street to the Kaiserkeller. George Harrison was 17 and was deported that November for being under age. They came back in 1961 and 1962, the last time to the Star-Club, which opened in April 1962. The Indra and the Kaiserkeller still trade as clubs. The Star-Club building is gone, and a memorial stone marks the site.

The Reeperbahn by night

After dark the street is what it has been for two hundred years: bars, clubs, theatres and sex shops, loud and very crowded on Friday and Saturday. A few plain rules help.

  • Keep your phone and wallet in a front pocket. Pickpockets work the crowd.
  • Do not photograph the women who work on the street or in Herbertstraße.
  • Glass bottles and weapons have been banned on the street on weekend nights, and the police presence is heavy.
  • With children, come by day.

The Landungsbrücken

Ten minutes downhill from the Reeperbahn is the river. The Landungsbrücken are floating pontoons nearly 700 metres long, built for the steamers of the liner age and reached by bridges from a stone terminal of 1909 with green domes and a tower that shows the water level. Walking them is free. The harbour ferries that leave from here belong to the city transport network: line 62, downstream to Finkenwerder and back, is a harbour trip for an ordinary ticket.

The Landungsbrücken from the water: the terminal of 1909 with its green domes. Photo: Thomas Dahlstrøm Nielsen, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Old Elbe Tunnel

The domed building at the western end of the pontoons is not a station. It is the top of a shaft. In 1911 Hamburg opened a tunnel under the Elbe for the thousands of dockers who crossed to the shipyards every day: two tubes, each about 426 metres long, some 24 metres below the surface. There were no ramps: carts and later cars were lowered in large lifts.

It still works that way, and for people on foot and on bicycles it is free at any hour. The walls are lined with glazed tiles, set with reliefs of fish, crabs and other things found in the river. On the far side, steps lead to a terrace with the best view back at the city. One tube at a time has been closed for restoration in recent years, and the other stays open.

One of the two tiled tubes of the Old Elbe Tunnel, opened in 1911. Photo: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The Rickmer Rickmers

The green three-master moored beside the pontoons was built in Bremerhaven in 1896 for the Rickmers shipping firm and named after a grandson of the family. She carried rice and bamboo from Asia. In 1916 Portugal seized her in the Azores, and she served the Portuguese navy as the training ship Sagres until the 1960s. She came home in 1983 and opened as a museum in 1987.

You go through the crew's quarters, the officers' saloon, the hold and the engine room, and out on deck under 97 metres of ship. Allow 45 minutes to an hour. The stairs are steep. A second museum ship, the white freighter Cap San Diego of 1961, lies five minutes to the east and has its own ticket.

Free, and not free

  • Free: the Reeperbahn and Große Freiheit, Beatles-Platz, the pontoons, the tunnel, the nave of St Michael's Church, the Sunday fish market by the river, which is over by mid-morning.
  • Ticket: the two museum ships, the tower of St Michael's, the Panoptikum, harbour boat tours, the theatres and clubs.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Rickmer Rickmers ticket with a city highlights audio tour is entry to the ship and an audio walk from there through the old town and the warehouse district. There is no commentary on board, and the escape room on the ship is excluded.
  • The Reeperbahn Nightscape audio tour is a walk of about a kilometre and a half from Große Freiheit to Millerntorplatz, in the partner's app, with the stories of the clubs, the theatres and the police station. A second walk, "Uncover Sinful Hamburg", covers nearly the same stops from the other end.
  • The harbour walk and "Maritime Charms" are audio routes along the quays. The first comes west from HafenCity to the Landungsbrücken. The second runs from the Elbphilharmonie past both museum ships and the tunnel to the fish market.
  • The Hamburg Dungeon ticket with an audio walk is a show with actors, in the warehouse district twenty minutes to the east, not in St. Pauli. The listing describes the show as in German and as unsuitable for children under ten.

None of the audio walks includes an entry. These are the tickets and walks our partner sells for St. Pauli and the harbour, with today's prices:

[partner city="hamburg" match="rickmer,reeperbahn,harbor,dungeon,maritime" limit="6"]

From here

St Michael's Church, the Michel, is ten minutes east of the pontoons. Its tower has a platform at 106 metres, by lift or by 452 steps. Hours are on our pages for the Rickmer Rickmers, Spielbudenplatz and St Michael's Church. See what else there is in Hamburg, or open the trip planner for Germany.

Cover photo: Dietmar Rabich, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is the Reeperbahn worth visiting during the day?
faqs.a: Yes, for its history: the theatres of Spielbudenplatz, the Davidwache police station, Große Freiheit and Beatles-Platz. It is quiet by day and suits a walk of an hour.

faqs.q: Is the Old Elbe Tunnel free?
faqs.a: Yes, for people on foot and on bicycles, at any hour. You go down by lift or stairs from the domed building at the Landungsbrücken.

faqs.q: Is the Rickmer Rickmers worth it?
faqs.a: If you like ships, yes. It is a three-masted cargo sailing ship of 1896 that you explore from the hold to the deck in 45 minutes to an hour.

faqs.q: Where did the Beatles play in Hamburg?
faqs.a: At the Indra and the Kaiserkeller on Große Freiheit in 1960, at the Top Ten Club on the Reeperbahn in 1961, and at the Star-Club in 1962. The Star-Club building no longer stands.

faqs.q: Is the Reeperbahn safe at night?
faqs.a: It is crowded and heavily policed, and most visitors have no trouble. Watch for pickpockets, do not photograph the sex workers, and visit by day if you are with children.

title: Potsdamer Platz in Berlin: the Panoramapunkt, the Spy Museum, the Deutschlandmuseum, and which to pay for
subtitle: A square that was a wasteland for forty years: what is left of the Wall, what is free, and three paid doors compared.
excerpt: What to see free on Potsdamer Platz (the Wall segments, the traffic tower, the old Sony Center), what the Panoramapunkt viewing platform, the German Spy Museum and the Deutschlandmuseum each offer, and what the partner tickets include.
longtail_phrases: is the Panoramapunkt in Berlin worth it
is the German Spy Museum worth visiting
what is the Deutschlandmuseum in Berlin
where can you see the Berlin Wall at Potsdamer Platz
Panoramapunkt or TV Tower Berlin
meta_title: Potsdamer Platz: Panoramapunkt, Spy Museum, which ticket
meta_description: What is free on Potsdamer Platz, and how the Panoramapunkt, the German Spy Museum and the Deutschlandmuseum compare before you pay for one of them.

featured_image.alt: The towers of Potsdamer Platz in Berlin at dusk, with the brown brick Kollhoff Tower in the middle between two glass high-rises

content_html:
[place attraction="potsdamer-platz" city="berlin"]

In the 1920s Potsdamer Platz was the busiest crossing in Germany. Five main streets met there, with trams, buses, cars and carts, and in 1924 the city put up a traffic tower in the middle: a five-sided steel post with a cabin at the top, from which a policeman worked the coloured lights by hand. It was among the first traffic lights in Europe.

Twenty years later the square was rubble. The borders of the Soviet, British and American sectors met on it, and in August 1961 the Wall was built straight across. For twenty-eight years the busiest crossing in Germany was an empty strip of sand and wire, the widest piece of border ground in the city centre. The Wall was opened here on 12 November 1989, and in the 1990s the wasteland became the largest building site in Europe. What stands there now is barely thirty years old. Three of its doors sell tickets, and a good deal else is free.

Potsdamer Platz in 1932, with the traffic tower in the middle of the crossing. Photo: Waldemar Titzenthaler, via Wikimedia Commons.

What is free on the square

  • The Wall segments. A short row of original concrete slabs stands on the pavement beside the station entrance, with panels that explain where you are. A double line of cobblestones set into the roadway marks where the Wall ran.
  • The traffic tower. A copy of the 1924 tower was put up in 1997, close to where the first one stood.
  • The tent roof. The complex built as the Sony Center, by Helmut Jahn, opened in 2000 around an oval court under a roof of fabric and glass. It has since been renamed and rebuilt inside. Walk in and look up. Fragments of the Esplanade, a grand hotel of 1908 that survived the war in part, were built into it behind glass.
  • Haus Huth. The pale stone building of 1912 among the glass ones is the only house that stood on the square through both the war and the Wall years.
  • Leipziger Platz. The eight-sided square next door, rebuilt on its old outline.

Segments of the Wall on the pavement of the square, beside the station entrance. Photo: Roland.h.bueb, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

More of the Wall, ten minutes away

The slabs on the square are a sample. For a longer piece, walk south-east to Niederkirchnerstraße, where about two hundred metres of the Wall still stand, pitted by the souvenir hunters of 1990. They run along the edge of the Topography of Terror, an open-air and indoor documentation centre on the ground where the Gestapo and the SS had their headquarters. Both are free. On the way, in a side street called Erna-Berger-Straße, stands one of the last East German watchtowers.

The Panoramapunkt

The brown brick high-rise with the stepped top is the Kollhoff Tower, finished in 1999 and a little over a hundred metres tall. A lift that the operator calls the fastest in Europe reaches the 24th floor in about twenty seconds. There is an open-air terrace on two levels, an outdoor exhibition about the history of the square, and a café.

The view is the reason to come. You are in the middle of the city, not on its edge: the Brandenburg Gate, the Reichstag and the Tiergarten lie to the north, the roofs of the Kulturforum just below to the west, and the TV Tower stands on the skyline to the east. Compared with the TV Tower you are lower, but outdoors, with no glass between you and the city, and the wait is usually short. Compared with the dome of the Reichstag, which is free but needs registration in advance, you can decide on the day. Go in clear weather, and expect wind. The terrace can close in a storm.

The copy of the traffic tower of 1924, put up in 1997. Photo: Marek Śliwecki, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The German Spy Museum

On Leipziger Platz, opened in 2015, a few metres from where the border ran. It tells the story of espionage from ancient ciphers to data collection today, with Cold War Berlin at the centre: an Enigma machine, cameras hidden in buttons and lipsticks, bugs, forged papers. Much of it is on screens and touch tables, and there is a room of laser beams to climb through against the clock.

Allow an hour and a half to two hours. It is the best of the three in rain, and the one children of about ten and over ask to stay in.

The Deutschlandmuseum

Two doors along, opened in 2023. It walks you through two thousand years of German history in twelve stage sets, from a forest of the Roman wars and a medieval castle to the 1920s and the divided country. There are sounds, screens and even smells, and the route is planned for about an hour.

Be clear about what it is. This is a private attraction that explains with scenery, not a collection of original objects. As a quick first orientation, or with teenagers, it does its job. If you want real things in cases, Berlin's state museums are the place.

Which to pay for

  • A clear day and one free hour: the Panoramapunkt.
  • Rain, or children: the Spy Museum.
  • A first day in Germany and little time: the Deutschlandmuseum.
  • Nothing: the Wall segments, the walk to the Topography of Terror, and the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe, eight minutes to the north.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Panoramapunkt admission ticket covers the lift, the terrace on both floors and the exhibition. Food and drink in the café are extra.
  • The VIP admission with coffee and cake adds a place in the fast lane for the lift and one coffee and one piece of cake. You exchange the voucher at the ticket office, and the café keeps its own hours.
  • The Berlin highlights tour with a Panoramapunkt ticket is the same entry with an audio walk of about four kilometres, in the partner's app, from the tower past the Brandenburg Gate and the Reichstag to the Red Town Hall. There is no commentary on the platform.
  • The historical journey with a German Spy Museum ticket is entry to the museum and that same audio walk. The listing says there is no audio guide inside.
  • The Deutschlandmuseum entry ticket is described as open-dated, with entry promised even on a busy day.

These are the tickets our partner sells on Potsdamer Platz and Leipziger Platz, with today's prices:

Getting there

Potsdamer Platz station has S-Bahn, U-Bahn and regional trains, all underground. The exits come up beside the Wall segments. Current hours are on our pages for Potsdamer Platz, the Spy Museum, the Deutschlandmuseum and the Topography of Terror.

From here

The Kulturforum, with the old masters of the Gemäldegalerie and the Neue Nationalgalerie, is ten minutes to the west. The Tiergarten begins across the road to the north, and the Brandenburg Gate is fifteen minutes away on foot along the line of the old border. See what else there is in Berlin, or open the trip planner for Germany.

Cover photo: Ansgar Koreng, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is the Panoramapunkt in Berlin worth it?
faqs.a: On a clear day, yes. It is an open-air terrace about a hundred metres up in the middle of the city, reached by a very fast lift, with the Brandenburg Gate, the Reichstag and the TV Tower in view.

faqs.q: Panoramapunkt or TV Tower: which view is better?
faqs.a: The TV Tower is much higher but behind glass and usually busier. The Panoramapunkt is lower, outdoors and central, and you can normally go up without planning ahead.

faqs.q: Is the German Spy Museum worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, in bad weather or with children of about ten and over. It is interactive, centred on Cold War Berlin, and takes an hour and a half to two hours.

faqs.q: What is the Deutschlandmuseum in Berlin?
faqs.a: A private attraction on Leipziger Platz, opened in 2023, that tells two thousand years of German history through twelve walk-through stage sets in about an hour. It is not a collection of original objects.

faqs.q: Where can you see the Berlin Wall at Potsdamer Platz?
faqs.a: A row of original segments stands beside the station entrance on the square. A stretch of about two hundred metres survives ten minutes away on Niederkirchnerstraße, by the Topography of Terror.

title: Bratislava as a day trip from Vienna: train, bus or boat, and what is free when you get there
subtitle: Two capitals an hour apart: how to cross, what to walk in five hours, and the few doors that ask for a ticket.

content_html:
[place attraction="bratislava-castle" city="bratislava"]

In 1914 an electric railway opened between Vienna and the town then called Pressburg in German and Pozsony in Hungarian. Its cars started near the centre of one city and ended in the streets of the other, and for a few years it was possible to go to the opera in Vienna and sleep at home on the Danube sixty kilometres downstream.

The town became Bratislava in 1919. The through service did not survive two wars and a new frontier, and after 1948 that frontier, which runs along the edge of the city's own suburbs, became part of the Iron Curtain: for forty years the two capitals were as far apart as two neighbours can be. Since the fences came down in 1989 the gap has closed again. Slovakia now uses the same currency as Austria and belongs to the same passport-free zone, and the journey takes about an hour.

Train, bus or boat

  • Train. The default. Regional trains leave Vienna's main station about every half hour and take around an hour. They alternate between two routes: one ends at Bratislava's main station, north of the old town, the other at Petržalka, south of the river. For a day on foot, take the first. Austrian railways have long sold a return ticket for this trip that also covers Bratislava's city transport: ask for it.
  • Bus. Several companies run coaches from Vienna, and from Vienna airport, in an hour to an hour and a quarter. They stop under the bridge at the edge of the old town or at the Nivy bus station. This is the choice if you are coming straight from a flight.
  • Boat. A fast catamaran runs in the warmer months from Schwedenplatz in the centre of Vienna to a pier beside Bratislava's old town, in about an hour and a quarter. It costs several times the train fare and needs booking. In return you pass the wetland forest of the Danube national park and, just before arriving, the castle ruin of Devín on its rock.

A good compromise is the boat one way and the train back. Our partner sells none of these journeys. Carry a passport or identity card: checks at the border are rare, but they do happen.

The old town, from the station

From the main station it is fifteen minutes downhill on foot, or a few stops by tram or bus. You pass the Grassalkovich Palace, the white residence of the Slovak president, and enter the old town through Michael's Gate, the only one of the medieval gates still standing. Its tower holds a small museum with a gallery at the top, and a ticket.

Michalská street runs down to the Main Square, with a fountain of 1572 and the Old Town Hall, whose tower you can climb as part of the city museum. One block east is the pink Primate's Palace. In its Hall of Mirrors, in December 1805, Austria signed the Peace of Pressburg after Napoleon's victory at Austerlitz. A small ticket lets you in, and shows you six English tapestries of the seventeenth century that were found behind a wall when the palace was restored.

Michalská street and Michael's Gate, the one medieval gate left. Photo: Fred Romero, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Houses on the Main Square, Hlavné námestie. Photo: Felix König, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

Statues and a coronation church

The streets south of the square are where the bronze figures are. The best known is Čumil, a workman leaning out of a manhole, placed there in 1997.

At the western edge of the old town stands St Martin's Cathedral. After the Ottomans took Buda, Pressburg served as the capital of the Kingdom of Hungary, and between 1563 and 1830 eleven Hungarian monarchs and eight of their consorts were crowned in this church, Maria Theresa among them in 1741. A gilded copy of the Hungarian crown sits on top of the spire instead of a cross. Entry to the nave has been free or nearly so.

Look at what runs past its door. In the late 1960s the approach road to a new bridge was driven between the cathedral and the castle hill, through the old Jewish quarter, and the synagogue that stood beside the church was pulled down.

Čumil, the Man at Work, on a street corner of the old town since 1997. Photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The castle: free outside, ticket inside

A footbridge or an underpass takes you across that road, and fifteen minutes of climbing bring you to the castle, a white block with four corner towers that people compare to an upturned table. It burned out in 1811 and stood as a ruin until it was rebuilt in the 1950s and 1960s.

The courtyard, the terraces and the Baroque garden are free. From the terrace you look over the Danube to the housing blocks of Petržalka and, beyond them, into Austria. Inside is the history museum of the Slovak National Museum, with a tower you can climb, on a ticket. On a short day, the outside is the better half.

The Blue Church and the bridge

The Church of St Elizabeth stands ten minutes east of the Main Square, outside the old core, and is missed by most groups. It was built between 1909 and 1913 by the Budapest architect Ödön Lechner, and everything about it is blue: walls, tiles, mosaics, even the pews. It is open only around services, in short windows in the morning and early evening, so on a day trip you may see it only from outside.

The bridge of 1972 has a round restaurant on top of its single leaning pylon, which gave it the name UFO. A lift goes up to a viewing deck, for a ticket.

The Church of St Elizabeth, the Blue Church, finished in 1913. Photo: Thomas Ledl, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What the partner sells: audio walks only

Our partner has no entry tickets and no transport for Bratislava. Its five listings are all self-guided audio walks in its app, on your own phone, with your own earphones. None includes an entry.

  • Historic Old Town and Castle: from SNP Square through the squares and past the cathedral up to the castle, about four kilometres. The closest match to the route above.
  • Old Town and Blue Church: from the Primate's Palace round the old town, ending at the Blue Church.
  • The communist era sites: from the castle steps to the bridge, the lost Jewish quarter and the squares of November 1989. The fee for the viewing deck is excluded.
  • Old Town Treasures and Riverside Charms: two longer loops that both use the bridge as one end. The second passes the Blue Church.

One is enough for a day. These are the audio walks our partner sells in Bratislava, with today's prices:

[partner city="bratislava" match="bratislava" limit="5"]

From here

With a spare two hours, a city bus from under the bridge reaches Devín Castle, the ruin you saw from the boat, where the Morava meets the Danube. Hours are on our pages for Bratislava Castle, the Blue Church and St Martin's Cathedral. See what else there is in Bratislava and in Vienna, or open the trip planner for Slovakia.

faqs.q: How do you get from Vienna to Bratislava?
faqs.a: By regional train from Vienna's main station in about an hour, by coach from the city or the airport in an hour to an hour and a quarter, or in the warmer months by fast catamaran from Schwedenplatz.

faqs.q: Is Bratislava worth a day trip from Vienna?
faqs.a: Yes. The old town is small enough to walk in five or six hours, with the castle terrace, the coronation cathedral and the Blue Church, and most of it is free.

faqs.q: Is Bratislava Castle free?
faqs.a: The courtyard, the terraces with the view and the Baroque garden are free. The history museum inside the castle needs a ticket.

faqs.q: How long do you need in Bratislava?
faqs.a: Five to six hours cover the old town, the castle and the Blue Church on foot. Add two hours if you want to go out to Devín Castle.

faqs.q: Is the boat from Vienna to Bratislava worth it?
faqs.a: For the ride, yes: it passes the Danube wetlands and Devín Castle and lands beside the old town. It costs several times the train fare, so many people take it one way only.
